propositions.text: From 1860s to 1990s, over 150,000 Indigenous children attended Indian Residential Schools funded by Canada and operated by religious groups.
propositions.quote: From the 1860s to the 1990s, more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit, and Métis children were required to attend Indian Residential Schools operated by religious organizations and funded by the Government of Canada.

propositions.text: Canada acknowledged the system aimed to remove children from their homes, families, traditions and culture.
propositions.quote: As Canada has acknowledged, this system was intended to “remove and isolate children from the influence of their homes, families, traditions and culture”

propositions.text: Thousands of children were physically, emotionally, and sexually abused at residential schools.
propositions.quote: Thousands of these children were abused physically, emotionally, and sexually while at residential schools.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states that from 1860s to 1990s, over 150,000 Indigenous children attended residential schools where many were abused.

propositions.text: Under the 2006 IRSSA, survivors could seek compensation through the Independent Assessment Process (IAP).
propositions.quote: Under the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (2006) (“IRSSA”), survivors of residential schools could seek compensation through the specially designed Independent Assessment Process (“IAP”).

propositions.text: IAP required claimants to disclose sensitive details of abuse and its consequences to an adjudicator.
propositions.quote: This entailed disclosure by claimants of acutely sensitive particulars — both of the abuse suffered, and of its consequences — for examination by an adjudicator.

propositions.text: IAP Documents include application forms, hearing transcripts, medical reports, decisions, and are held by Canada.
propositions.quote: This information is recorded in application forms, hearing transcripts, medical reports, reasons for decisions and other documents (collectively, the “IAP Documents”), copies of which are held by Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the IRSSA's IAP process requires sensitive disclosures recorded in IAP Documents held by Canada.

propositions.text: The appeal concerns whether IAP Documents should be destroyed or archived at Library and Archives Canada.
propositions.quote: This appeal concerns the fate of the digital and physical records generated by this process. In particular, this Court must determine whether the IAP Documents should be destroyed, or retained and eventually archived at Library and Archives Canada.

propositions.text: The supervising judge ordered destruction of IAP Documents after 15 years, allowing claimants to preserve their own files.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge found that these records must be destroyed following a 15-year retention period during which individual IAP claimants could elect to have the records in their own file preserved.

propositions.text: Ontario Court of Appeal majority upheld the supervising judge’s destruction order.
propositions.quote: This order was substantially upheld by the majority of the Ontario Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: The Attorney General of Canada appeals the destruction order to this Court.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada now appeals that result to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns whether IAP Documents should be destroyed or archived; lower courts ordered destruction; Canada appeals.

propositions.text: The Court would dismiss the appeal and uphold the supervising judge’s order as varied by the Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: We would dismiss the appeal and uphold the supervising judge’s order as varied by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: The supervising judge’s order is not precluded by the Library and Archives of Canada Act or other legislation.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge’s order is not, as the Attorney General of Canada claims, precluded by the operation of the Library and Archives of Canada Act, S.C. 2004, c. 11 , or any other legislation.

propositions.text: The supervising judge properly exercised discretionary power to administer the IRSSA.
propositions.quote: it was an appropriate exercise of the supervising judge’s discretionary power to administer the IRSSA.

paragraphs.summary: The Court would dismiss the appeal, finding the destruction order lawful and a proper exercise of discretion.

propositions.text: In late 1990s and early 2000s, individual and class actions were brought by residential school survivors.
propositions.quote: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, a number of individual and class actions were brought by survivors of residential schools.

propositions.text: In 2003, Canada established a voluntary ADR process to compensate survivors.
propositions.quote: In November 2003, the Government of Canada established a voluntary alternative dispute resolution (“ADR”) process to compensate survivors.

propositions.text: In 2006, class actions were consolidated into a single action and the IRSSA was reached.
propositions.quote: In 2006, an agreement was reached and class actions in nine provinces and territories were consolidated into a single action.

propositions.text: The IRSSA is a comprehensive settlement negotiated by plaintiffs, Canada, and religious organizations.
propositions.quote: The IRSSA is a comprehensive settlement of that class action, and was the product of extensive negotiations among the plaintiffs and their representatives, the Government of Canada, and various religious organizations which had operated these schools.

propositions.text: The IRSSA aims for fair resolution, healing, education, truth, reconciliation, and commemoration.
propositions.quote: It seeks to achieve a “fair, comprehensive and lasting resolution of the legacy of Indian Residential Schools” and aims to promote “healing, education, truth and reconciliation and commemoration”

propositions.text: The IRSSA provides compensation, establishes a truth and reconciliation commission, funds healing programs, and resolves litigation.
propositions.quote: by: (1) financially compensating former students of residential schools; (2) establishing a truth and reconciliation commission; (3) providing an endowment to healing programs; and (4) resolving all outstanding litigation regarding residential schools.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the IRSSA's background: class actions consolidated, settlement negotiated, and its aims and components.

propositions.text: IRSSA compensation has two forms: Common Experience Payment (CEP) and Independent Assessment Process (IAP).
propositions.quote: Compensation under the IRSSA may take two forms. First, the Common Experience Payment (“CEP”) ... The second manner ... is through the IAP.

propositions.text: CEP provides $10,000 plus $3,000 per additional year for eligible claimants.
propositions.quote: The Common Experience Payment (“CEP”) provides $10,000 to eligible claimants who resided at an Indian Residential School for one school year or part thereof, and an additional $3,000 for every additional year or part thereof

propositions.text: IAP compensates survivors of sexual, serious physical abuse, and other wrongful acts causing serious psychological harm.
propositions.quote: The second manner by which claimants may be compensated ... is through the IAP. It allows former students who were survivors of sexual abuse, serious physical abuse, and other wrongful acts resulting in serious psychological consequences to bring claims forward

propositions.text: IAP application deadline was September 19, 2012; by June 2014, 37,716 claims initiated, 25,800 resolved.
propositions.quote: The deadline for applying to the IAP was September 19, 2012. As of June 2014, 37,716 IAP claims had been initiated, of which 25,800 had been resolved.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains IRSSA compensation forms: CEP and IAP, with IAP claims statistics as of 2014.

propositions.text: IAP claimants submit application forms detailing abuse, alleged perpetrators, and compensation requests.
propositions.quote: The IAP begins with an application that appears to serve functions similar to a statement of claim. In the application form, the Claimant provides details of the wrongdoing with dates, places, times, and the Claimant provides information to identify the alleged perpetrator.

propositions.text: Applications include a first-person narrative and required documents depending on claim nature.
propositions.quote: In the application, the Claimant provides a Narrative in the first person and outlines his or her request for compensation in accordance with the IRSSA. Depending on the nature of the claim for compensation, certain documents must be provided by a Claimant with the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the IAP application process requiring detailed personal narratives and supporting documents.

propositions.text: Claimants disclose intimate personal information in IAP applications.
propositions.quote: for a claimant to complete the application form, he or she will disclose the most private and most intimate personal information, including a first-person narrative outlining his or her request for compensation

propositions.text: Applications are forwarded to Canada and the church entity operating the relevant residential school.
propositions.quote: Applications are then forwarded to Canada and to the church entity that operated the residential school in question.

propositions.text: If not settled, claims proceed to a hearing before an adjudicator supervised by the Chief Adjudicator.
propositions.quote: If the claim is not settled at this stage, it will proceed to a hearing before an adjudicator, supervised by the Chief Adjudicator of the Indian Residential Schools Adjudication Secretariat.

propositions.text: The Settlement Agreement Operations Branch represents Canada as defendant in claims.
propositions.quote: The Settlement Agreement Operations Branch (“SAO”), a branch within Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada (“AANDC”), represents Canada as a defendant to these claims.

propositions.text: IAP hearings are private; attendees must sign confidentiality agreements.
propositions.quote: The Secretariat’s website at the time of the requests for directions represented that IAP hearings are private: “The hearing is held in private. The public and the media are not allowed to attend. Each person who attends the hearing must sign a confidentiality agreement. This means that what is said at the hearing stays private”

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found IAP applications disclose intimate information, hearings are private, and Canada and churches receive applications.

propositions.text: IAP hearings test claimant credibility and assess harm suffered.
propositions.quote: IAP hearings serve two purposes: testing the credibility of the claimant and assessing the harm suffered.

propositions.text: Adjudicators produce decisions outlining factual findings and rationale for compensation entitlement.
propositions.quote: After the hearing, the adjudicator produces a decision outlining key factual findings and, generally, the adjudicator must outline the rationale for finding or not finding that the claimant is entitled to compensation.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found IAP hearings assess credibility and harm, with adjudicators issuing reasoned decisions.

propositions.text: IAP Documents include seven categories: applications, mandatory documents, witness statements, evidence, transcripts, expert reports, and decisions.
propositions.quote: the IAP Documents comprise seven categories: “(1) applications submitted by the claimants; (2) mandatory documents containing private personal information; (3) witness statements; (4) documentary evidence produced by the parties; (5) transcripts and audio recordings of the hearings; (6) expert and medical reports; and (7) decisions of the adjudicators and any appeals”

propositions.text: Thousands of digital and physical copies of IAP Documents exist for over 37,000 claims.
propositions.quote: The Secretariat and the SAO both currently possess thousands of digital and physical copies of these various records pertaining to more than 37,000 claims made under the IAP.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found IAP Documents include seven categories and thousands of copies exist for over 37,000 claims.

propositions.text: IRSSA also aims to commemorate and memorialize residential schools through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).
propositions.quote: beyond its compensation function, the IRSSA also aims to commemorate and memorialize the residential schools system. Article 7.01 of the IRSSA established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (“TRC”).

propositions.text: The TRC creates a historical record and ensures its legacy is preserved and accessible to the public.
propositions.quote: The TRC is tasked with “creat[ing] a historical record of the residential school system and ensur[ing that] its legacy is preserved and made accessible to the public for future study and use”

propositions.text: The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR) archives and stores TRC records and historical residential school records.
propositions.quote: The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (“NCTR”) was to archive and store the records collected by the TRC, along with the historical records regarding residential schools.

propositions.text: There is tension between commemoration and claimant privacy promised in IAP.
propositions.quote: The tension between that mandate of commemoration and memorialization, and the privacy which IAP claimants were promised, lies at the heart of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found IRSSA established the TRC and NCTR to preserve records, creating tension with IAP claimant privacy.

propositions.text: Chief Adjudicator and TRC requested directions from Ontario Superior Court on disposition of IAP Documents and notice program.
propositions.quote: The Chief Adjudicator and the TRC brought requests for directions to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on the disposition of the IAP Documents and, if necessary, on the development of a notice program to inform claimants of the possibility of voluntarily archiving some of their IAP Documents at the NCTR.

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Adjudicator and TRC sought court directions on IAP Documents disposition and notice program development.

propositions.text: TRC argued IAP Documents are government records subject to Library and Archives of Canada Act.
propositions.quote: The TRC argued that the IAP Documents were government records under its control, and therefore subject to the Library and Archives of Canada Act .

propositions.text: Canada and NCTR supported TRC, saying IAP Documents are essential to preserving historical record.
propositions.quote: Canada and the NCTR generally supported the TRC’s position, arguing that the IAP Documents are essential to preserving the historical record of the residential school abuses.

propositions.text: Chief Adjudicator said IAP Documents are court records, not government records, and should be destroyed after retention period.
propositions.quote: The Chief Adjudicator, however, submitted that the IAP Documents were court records, not government records. The intention underlying the IRSSA was that the IAP Documents should be destroyed after a retention period to allow for voluntary archival by the claimant.

propositions.text: Assembly of First Nations, Catholic Entities, and Independent Counsel generally supported destruction after retention period.
propositions.quote: This call for destruction, following a retention period, was generally echoed by the Assembly of First Nations, the Sisters of St. Joseph of Sault Ste. Marie, the Twenty-Four Catholic Entities, the Nine Catholic Entities, and the Independent Counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The TRC, Canada, and NCTR argued IAP Documents are government records; Chief Adjudicator and others supported destruction after retention.

propositions.text: Supervising judge reviewed IRSSA contractual interpretation principles focusing on parties' intent and context.
propositions.quote: The supervising judge, Perell J., began by reviewing the principles of contractual interpretation applicable to the IRSSA, which entails identifying the intent of the parties at the time they negotiated the contract.

propositions.text: He adopted Fontaine 2013 ONSC 684 principles: read agreement as whole, consider plain meaning and context.
propositions.quote: He adopted the principles of interpretation applicable to the IRSSA as stated in Fontaine v. Canada (Attorney General), 2013 ONSC 684, 114 O.R. (3d) 263, at para. 68, that the text of the agreement must be read as whole, having regard to the plain meaning of the words used as well as the context provided by the circumstances existing at the time the IRSSA was created.

propositions.text: IRSSA is not a treaty but is at least as important; interpretation must be informed by honour of the Crown.
propositions.quote: he observed that the IRSSA, while not a treaty, “is at least as important as a treaty” and its interpretation must be informed by the honour of the Crown (para. 88).

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge applied contractual interpretation principles to IRSSA, emphasizing honour of the Crown.

propositions.text: Supervising judge concluded court should order destruction of IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: On balance, the supervising judge concluded that the court should exercise its jurisdiction to order destruction of the IAP Documents.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge concluded the court should order destruction of the IAP Documents.

propositions.text: First, destruction aligns with parties' bargain for confidentiality in IRSSA.
propositions.quote: First, as a matter of contractual interpretation, destruction is what the parties had bargained for. The IAP was intended to be a confidential process, and both claimants and alleged perpetrators had relied on that assurance of confidentiality in deciding to participate.

propositions.text: Archiving at Library and Archives Canada would breach the high confidentiality bargained for.
propositions.quote: Archiving the IAP Documents at Library and Archives Canada would not conform to the “high degree of confidentiality that the parties bargained for”

propositions.text: IRSSA provides for destruction after retention period governed by Access to Information and Privacy Acts.
propositions.quote: the IRSSA provided that the IAP Documents, including Canada’s copies thereof, would be destroyed following a retention period, during which period they would be governed by the Access to Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. A-1 , and the Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21 .

propositions.text: Alternatively, destruction is an implied term necessary for operative efficiency of IRSSA.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, destruction of the IAP Documents amounted to an implied term in the IRSSA, because it was necessary to give the agreement “operative efficiency”

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found destruction was bargained for confidentiality, required by IRSSA, or implied for efficiency.

propositions.text: Second, IAP Documents are subject to an implied undertaking enforceable by destruction order.
propositions.quote: Second, the IAP Documents are subject to an implied undertaking, which the court can enforce by ordering their destruction.

propositions.text: Court has jurisdiction to order destruction despite Canada’s possession, as IAP is a form of litigation with implied undertaking.
propositions.quote: the court had jurisdiction to make an order in rem that the IAP Documents be destroyed, subject to the rights of claimants to archive them at the NCTR, because “[t]he IAP Documents are a product of an alternative dispute resolution mechanism”

propositions.text: Implied undertaking restricts Canada from sharing IAP Documents with TRC, NCTR, or Library and Archives Canada.
propositions.quote: this implied undertaking restricted Canada from providing its IAP Documents to the TRC, the NCTR, or Library and Archives Canada, and the court could order destruction of all the IAP Documents to enforce the implied undertaking.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found an implied undertaking applies to IAP Documents, allowing court to order destruction to enforce confidentiality.

propositions.text: Third, IAP Documents are protected by breach of confidence law; breach occurred by transferring to Library and Archives Canada.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge found that Canada’s agreement to transfer the IAP Documents to Library and Archives Canada amounted to a breach of confidence

propositions.text: Breach of confidence occurs when confidential info is misused by confidant under obligation of confidentiality.
propositions.quote: “A breach of confidence occurs when a confider discloses confidential information to a confidant in circumstances in which there is an obligation of confidentiality and the confidant misuses the confidential information”

propositions.text: The appropriate remedy for breach was destruction after 15-year retention period.
propositions.quote: the appropriate remedy was an order providing for destruction after a 15-year retention period.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found breach of confidence law protects IAP Documents and ordered destruction as remedy.

propositions.text: Destruction order should include a retention period allowing notice program to inform claimants about archiving rights.
propositions.quote: his destruction order should be made subject to a retention period. This would allow for the development and implementation of a notice program, conducted by the TRC or the NCTR, to advise IAP claimants of the rights they have under the IRSSA to share their stories with the NCTR.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge ordered destruction after a retention period to allow notice program informing claimants of archiving rights.

propositions.text: Catholic Entities argued IRSSA requires their consent for archiving, not just claimant consent.
propositions.quote: the Sisters of St. Joseph of Sault Ste. Marie, the Twenty-Two Catholic Entities, and the Nine Catholic Entities, supported by the Independent Counsel, argued that the IRSSA expressly provides that archiving requires their consent, and not just that of a claimant.

propositions.text: Canada argued it controls IAP Documents, subject to federal privacy, access, and archiving laws.
propositions.quote: Canada, on cross-appeal, supported by the TRC and NCTR, argued that it controls the IAP Documents, which are accordingly subject to federal privacy, access to information, and archiving legislation.

propositions.text: Independent Counsel argued notice program should be run by Chief Adjudicator, retention period lowered to 2 years, and destruction include ADR documents.
propositions.quote: Independent Counsel, in addition to supporting the Catholic Entities’ submission regarding consent, argued that the notice program should not be run by either the TRC or NCTR, but by the Chief Adjudicator. Further, the retention period for the IAP Documents should be lowered to 2 years from 15 years. Finally, the destruction order should include documents from the ADR process.

paragraphs.summary: The Catholic Entities, Canada, and Independent Counsel made submissions on consent, control, notice program, retention period, and scope of destruction.

propositions.text: Strathy C.J. dismissed both appeal and cross-appeal but varied Perell J.'s order on notice program and ADR documents.
propositions.quote: Strathy C.J. dismissed both the appeal and cross-appeal. Nonetheless, he varied Perell J.’s order to give effect to the Independent Counsel’s submissions on the notice program (that it should be administered by the Chief Adjudicator) and on the inclusion of the ADR documents.

paragraphs.summary: Strathy C.J. dismissed appeal and cross-appeal but varied Perell J.'s order on notice program and ADR documents, court states.

propositions.text: IAP Documents may be archived with claimant's consent alone under IRSSA Schedule D.
propositions.quote: the majority concluded that the IAP Documents may be archived with the consent of the claimant alone. Schedule D of the IRSSA gives claimants the option of having a transcript from their hearing deposited in an archive for that purpose.

propositions.text: IRSSA permits survivors to disclose their experiences despite confidentiality claims by others.
propositions.quote: The IRSSA permits survivors to disclose their own experiences, despite any claims that others may make with respect to confidentiality and privacy.

propositions.text: Requiring consent of other individuals for archiving would eviscerate claimants' IRSSA rights.
propositions.quote: Requiring consent of other “individuals affected” for archiving of the IAP Documents would “eviscerate” claimants’ IRSSA rights to disclose their complaints, to have their evidence archived only with their consent, and to exercise control over their IAP Documents

propositions.text: Allowing claimants to archive transcripts provides an alternative means to preserve their stories in the TRC process.
propositions.quote: By allowing claimants to archive their IAP transcripts, the IRSSA merely provides claimants with an alternative and expeditious means of preserving their stories as part of the TRC process

paragraphs.summary: Court finds IAP Documents may be archived with claimant consent alone; IRSSA permits survivors to disclose experiences despite others' confidentiality claims.

propositions.text: Notice plan falls within supervising judge's administrative discretion and is not a material amendment to IRSSA.
propositions.quote: The majority further concluded the notice plan fell within the supervising judge’s administrative discretion, as it was not a material amendment to the IRSSA.

propositions.text: Schedule D contemplates claimants will be given option to archive transcripts.
propositions.quote: Schedule D expressly contemplates that claimants “will . . . be given the option of having the transcript deposited in an archive developed for the purpose”.

propositions.text: IRSSA gives claimants right to obtain and deposit IAP documents and transcripts in NCTR.
propositions.quote: [T]he IRSSA gives claimants the right to obtain their IAP documents and a transcript of their evidence, and the right to deposit that material in the institution created to preserve the history of the abuses of residential schools, the NCTR

propositions.text: Notice program ensures claimants are aware of and able to exercise their rights; it neither adds nor detracts.
propositions.quote: The notice program does not add to or detract from this right; “it merely ensures that claimants are aware of it and able to exercise it”

paragraphs.summary: Court finds notice plan within judge's discretion; IRSSA contemplates transcript archiving; notice program ensures claimants' awareness and exercise of rights.

propositions.text: IAP Documents are not government records and not subject to Library and Archives of Canada Act.
propositions.quote: the majority found that the IAP Documents are not government records and thus are not subject to the Library and Archives of Canada Act ; accordingly, “disposal or destruction of the documents is not prohibited by law”

propositions.text: Whether IAP Documents are government records depends on control by government institution.
propositions.quote: [W]hether the IAP documents are government records . . . turns on whether they are under the control of a government institution

propositions.text: IAP was court-approved settlement, not federal government program.
propositions.quote: Here, the IAP was not a federal government program. Rather, it was the product of a court-approved settlement.

propositions.text: AANDC did not control IAP Documents through Secretariat or SAO.
propositions.quote: The AANDC, a listed government institution, did not control the IAP Documents through either the Secretariat or the SAO.

propositions.text: Secretariat is independent from AANDC and under Chief Adjudicator's control.
propositions.quote: The Secretariat, which administers the IAP, is independent from AANDC and comes under the direction of the Chief Adjudicator, and therefore the control of the Chief Adjudicator.

propositions.text: SAO, part of AANDC, was litigant representing Canada and had limited possession and use of IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: While the SAO is part of the AANDC, it was a litigant in the IAP, representing Canada at the IAP hearings. Accordingly, the SAO’s possession and use of the IAP Documents was limited to the purposes for which they were provided.

propositions.text: SAO did not control IAP Documents; possession constrained by court's inherent jurisdiction and implied undertaking rule rationale.
propositions.quote: It follows that it did not control them. Strathy C.J. also held that while “the implied undertaking rule is not a precise fit for the IAP documents”, the rationale underlying the rule is, given the nature of these documents, “a harmonious exercise of the court’s inherent jurisdiction”

propositions.text: SAO could only use IAP Documents for IAP process; possession constrained by court's jurisdiction and implied undertaking rule principle.
propositions.quote: The SAO could only use the IAP Documents for the purpose of the IAP process, and its possession was always constrained by the court’s inherent jurisdiction and the principle underlying the implied undertaking rule.

propositions.text: IAP Documents were not under SAO control.
propositions.quote: Thus, this reaffirms that the IAP Documents were not under the control of the SAO.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds IAP Documents not government records; AANDC and SAO did not control them; SAO's possession limited and constrained by court jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Supervising judge's order to destroy IAP Documents after 15 years (except claimant-held or archived) was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The majority further found the supervising judge’s order regarding destruction of all the IAP Documents (other than those in the claimants’ possession or archived with their consent) after a 15-year retention period was reasonable.

propositions.text: IRSSA silent on document disposition; supervising judge entitled to fill gap by supervisory authority.
propositions.quote: The IRSSA was silent on the disposition of the documents, and the supervising judge was entitled to fill this “gap” by exercising his supervisory authority over the class action

propositions.text: Near absolute confidentiality was necessary for IAP.
propositions.quote: As the supervising judge found, “near to absolute confidentiality was a necessary aspect of the IAP”

propositions.text: Schedule D's lack of immediate destruction requirement does not imply right to retain forever.
propositions.quote: The mere fact that Sch. D did not require Canada to destroy the applications immediately upon conclusion of a given claim does not imply or import a right to retain all the IAP Documents forever.

propositions.text: Public record preserved through TRC's work despite destruction of IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: The public record — that is, “the history of residential school and the stories of survivors who have willingly shared them” — will still be preserved through the work of the TRC

paragraphs.summary: Court finds supervising judge's order to destroy IAP Documents after 15 years reasonable; IRSSA silent on disposition; confidentiality necessary; TRC preserves public record.

propositions.text: Supervising judge's order for TRC and NCTR to conduct notice program was unreasonable; order varied to Chief Adjudicator.
propositions.quote: The majority, nevertheless, found it was unreasonable for the supervising judge to have ordered the TRC and NCTR to conduct the notice program, and varied the order to direct that it be conducted by the Chief Adjudicator.

propositions.text: Order varied to include ADR documents.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the majority varied the order to include the ADR documents.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds supervising judge's order for TRC and NCTR to conduct notice program unreasonable; varied to Chief Adjudicator and included ADR documents.

propositions.text: Justice Sharpe agreed appeal dismissal but would allow cross-appeal that IAP Documents are government records.
propositions.quote: Justice Sharpe, while agreeing that the appeal should be dismissed, would have allowed the cross-appeal on the ground that the IAP Documents are “government records”

propositions.text: SAO is government institution with physical possession of IAP Documents as government department defendant in IAP, amounting to government control.
propositions.quote: The SAO is a government institution that has physical possession of copies of the IAP Documents in its capacity as the department of government responsible for carrying out Canada’s functions as a defendant in the IAP. This amounts to government control.

propositions.text: Implied undertaking rule and breach of confidence do not apply to IAP Documents as government records.
propositions.quote: The legal doctrines relied on by the supervising judge — the implied undertaking rule and breach of confidence — therefore have no application, and do not affect the status of the IAP Documents as government records.

propositions.text: Destruction of decisions central to legitimacy of process should not rely on residual, discretionary doctrine.
propositions.quote: Resort should not been had “to a residual, discretionary and exceptional doctrine to justify the destruction of decisions that are central to the legitimacy of the very process the court is administering”

paragraphs.summary: Justice Sharpe dissents on cross-appeal, finding IAP Documents are government records under SAO control; implied undertaking rule inapplicable; destruction unjustified.

propositions.text: Justice Sharpe found IRSSA language shows IAP Documents intended to be archived.
propositions.quote: Justice Sharpe also found that express language in the IRSSA shows that the parties intended that the IAP Documents would be archived.

propositions.text: Schedule D, App. II, item (iv) provides copies other than government-held will be destroyed.
propositions.quote: Schedule D, App. II, item (iv) provides that copies of applications “other than those held by the Government will be destroyed”.

propositions.text: Guide to IAP Application states only National Archivist can destroy government records.
propositions.quote: Appendix B of the Guide to the Independent Assessment Process Application (2013) (online) provides that only the National Archivist can destroy government records.

propositions.text: Personal information handled per Access to Information Act and Privacy Act.
propositions.quote: The Guide states that personal information will be handled in accordance with the Access to Information Act and Privacy Act .

propositions.text: Confidentiality assurances cannot exclude documents from statutory scheme; laws apply to IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: In the result, assurances of confidentiality, relied upon by the supervising judge, cannot justify the exclusion of documents from the statutory scheme. IAP adjudicators could not promise that the laws of Canada would not apply, and Canada could not promise a level of confidentiality that would take the IAP Documents outside the reach of the legislation.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Sharpe finds IRSSA language shows IAP Documents intended to be archived; confidentiality assurances cannot exclude them from statutory laws.

propositions.text: Whether supervising judge had authority to order disposition of IAP Documents under IRSSA is first question before Court.
propositions.quote: The first question before this Court is therefore whether the supervising judge had authority to make that order.

propositions.text: This question is distinct from appropriateness of the order.
propositions.quote: This question is distinct from the appropriateness of the order.

paragraphs.summary: Court states first issue is whether supervising judge had authority to order disposition of IAP Documents under IRSSA, distinct from order's appropriateness.

propositions.text: Canada argues IAP Documents in SAO and Secretariat possession are under government institution control under federal statutes.
propositions.quote: Canada argues that the IAP Documents currently in the possession of the SAO and the Secretariat are “under the control of a government institution”, within the meaning of the Access to Information Act , the Privacy Act , and the Library and Archives of Canada Act .

propositions.text: Canada says supervising judge had no jurisdiction to order destruction due to s. 12 of Library and Archives of Canada Act.
propositions.quote: In Canada’s view, the supervising judge had no jurisdiction to order destruction of the IAP Documents, because s. 12 of the Library and Archives of Canada Act provides that “[n]o government or ministerial record . . . shall be disposed of, including by being destroyed, without the written consent of the Librarian and Archivist or of a person to whom the Librarian and Archivist has, in writing, delegated the power to give such consents.”

propositions.text: Only Librarian and Archivist or delegate has authority over disposition of IAP Documents retained by SAO and Secretariat.
propositions.quote: In other words, Canada’s position is that, given the government’s putative “control” over these documents, the Librarian and Archivist of Canada (or his or her delegate) alone has authority over the disposition of the IAP Documents retained by the SAO and the Secretariat, and so the supervising judge could not order their destruction.

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues IAP Documents in SAO and Secretariat possession are government-controlled; only Librarian and Archivist can authorize destruction; supervising judge lacked jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Nine provincial and territorial superior courts certified class action and approved IRSSA; judges designated supervising judges.
propositions.quote: nine provincial and territorial superior courts certified the class action and approved the IRSSA (see, e.g., Baxter). Judges of these courts were designated as supervising judges

propositions.text: Supervising judges have administrative and supervisory jurisdiction over IRSSA implementation and can hear requests for directions.
propositions.quote: Supervising judges, significantly, have administrative and supervisory jurisdiction over the implementation and administration of the IRSSA and can, among other things, hear requests for directions.

propositions.text: Supervising judges empowered to give directions necessary for proper administration and implementation of IRSSA.
propositions.quote: If, therefore, the proper administration and implementation of the IRSSA necessitates direction on the handling of the IAP Documents, supervising judges are empowered to give that direction.

paragraphs.summary: Court states nine superior courts certified class action and approved IRSSA; supervising judges have jurisdiction to direct IRSSA implementation including IAP Documents handling.

propositions.text: Broad powers conferred on supervising judges by orders approving IRSSA and class action legislation.
propositions.quote: These broad powers are conferred upon supervising judges by the orders which approved and implemented the IRSSA (see, e.g., supervising judge’s reasons, at paras. 157-59). They are also supported by class action legislation

propositions.text: Class action legislation provides courts generous discretion to make orders for fair and expeditious resolution.
propositions.quote: class action legislation, which provides that courts must have generous discretion to make orders and impose terms as necessary to ensure a fair and expeditious resolution of class actions (see, e.g., Class Proceedings Act, 1992, S.O. 1992, c. 6, s. 12; Endean v. British Columbia, 2016 SCC 42, [2016] 2 S.C.R. 162, at para. 38).

propositions.text: Supervisory role includes making directions on disposition of IAP Documents at IAP conclusion.
propositions.quote: It follows, particularly given the nature of the IAP and the IAP Documents, that the supervisory role in implementing the terms of the IRSSA included making directions regarding disposition of the IAP Documents at the conclusion of the IAP.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds supervising judges have broad powers under IRSSA and class action law, including directing disposition of IAP Documents at IAP conclusion.

propositions.text: Supervisory role exists regardless of whether IAP Documents are government records under federal legislation.
propositions.quote: This supervisory role, moreover, existed irrespective of whether the IAP Documents are “under the control of a government institution” within the meaning of the Library and Archives of Canada Act and other relevant federal legislation

propositions.text: Superior courts retain residual supervisory powers under inherent jurisdiction unless clear statutory language removes it.
propositions.quote: superior courts retain residual supervisory powers under their inherent jurisdiction. Removing the inherent jurisdiction of superior courts requires “clear and precise statutory language” (R. v. Rose, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 262, at para. 133; see also Endean, at paras. 24, 56 and 60).

propositions.text: Library and Archives of Canada Act does not mandate retention nor prevent courts from ordering disposition of government records.
propositions.quote: The Library and Archives of Canada Act does not mandate the retention of government records, nor does it prevent the courts from making orders regarding the disposition of government records.

propositions.text: Supervising judge correctly found he had authority to order disposition of IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: In sum, the supervising judge correctly found that he had authority to make orders as to the disposition of the IAP Documents.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds supervisory role exists regardless of government record status; superior courts retain inherent jurisdiction; supervising judge had authority to order disposition.

propositions.text: Unnecessary to determine if IAP Documents are government records given supervisory role allows disposition orders regardless.
propositions.quote: In light of this conclusion, it is unnecessary to determine whether the IAP Documents are under the control of a government institution, as Canada argues.

propositions.text: Court will consider supervising judge's IRSSA interpretation and order appropriateness next.
propositions.quote: We therefore turn to consider the basis for the supervising judge’s order itself — that is, his interpretation of the IRSSA — and whether, in light of that interpretation, the order for destruction of the IAP Documents was appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no need to decide if IAP Documents are government records; will next consider supervising judge's IRSSA interpretation and order appropriateness.

propositions.text: Interpretation of IRSSA is mixed fact and law, reviewable for palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: The interpretation of the IRSSA is a question of mixed fact and law reviewable for palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation generally involves mixed fact and law, subject to appellate deference (Sattva).
propositions.quote: Contractual interpretation generally involves questions of mixed fact and law subject to appellate deference (Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., 2014 SCC 53, [2014] 2 S.C.R. 633, at paras. 50-51 and 55; Heritage Capital Corp. v. Equitable Trust Co., 2016 SCC 19, [2016] 1 S.C.R. 306, at para. 21).

propositions.text: Exception to deference for standard form contracts with no factual matrix (Ledcor).
propositions.quote: This rule is not absolute. It does not apply, for example, to the interpretation of a standard form contract, where its interpretation has precedential value, and there is no meaningful factual matrix specific to the particular parties to assist the interpretation process (Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., 2016 SCC 37, [2016] 2 S.C.R. 23, at para. 46).

propositions.text: Palpable and overriding error standard governs appellate review of supervising judge's IRSSA interpretation here.
propositions.quote: In our view, however, the general rule stated in Sattva applies here, such that the palpable and overriding error standard governs appellate review of the supervising judge’s interpretation of the IRSSA.

propositions.text: IRSSA is a contract whose meaning depends on objective intentions of parties; factual matrix important.
propositions.quote: While the IRSSA undoubtedly has “very significant implications for Canada and our aboriginal peoples” (C.A. reasons, at para. 294), it is at root a contract, the meaning of which depends on the objective intentions of the parties.

propositions.text: Supervising judge's IRSSA interpretation impacts many claimants but has no significant precedential value outside IAP.
propositions.quote: While the supervising judge’s interpretation of the IRSSA will impact thousands of IAP claimants, it will have no significant precedential value outside of the IAP due to the IRSSA’s sui generis nature.

propositions.text: Factual matrix is significant in interpreting this contract.
propositions.quote: And, as shall become apparent below, the factual matrix looms large in ascertaining the meaning of this particular contract.

paragraphs.summary: Court states IRSSA interpretation is mixed fact and law, reviewable for palpable error; IRSSA is contract with important factual matrix; no broad precedential value.

propositions.text: Supervising judge's order to destroy IAP Documents after 15 years reviewed with deference.
propositions.quote: As for the supervising judge’s decision to order destruction of the IAP Documents held by Canada following a 15-year retention period, a deferential standard is also appropriate.

propositions.text: Supervisory courts have wide discretion to make orders for fair and expeditious class proceedings; appellate intervention only for clear error or injustice.
propositions.quote: Such decisions are afforded deference on review (Lavier v. MyTravel Canada Holidays Inc., 2013 ONCA 92, 359 D.L.R. (4th) 713, at para. 20). As regards the exercise of discretion, “[a]ppellate intervention is warranted only if the judge has clearly misdirected himself or herself on the facts or the law, proceeded arbitrarily, or if the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice”

propositions.text: Appellate reviewers must generally defer if first instance judge gave sufficient weight and did not err in principle.
propositions.quote: As this Court has said, where the judge at first instance has given sufficient weight to all relevant considerations and the exercise of discretion is not based on an erroneous principle, appellate reviewers must generally defer

paragraphs.summary: Court states supervising judge's destruction order reviewed with deference; appellate intervention only for clear error or injustice.

propositions.text: Contractual interpretation grounded in text and entire contract; surrounding circumstances may be considered but not overwhelm express words.
propositions.quote: Interpretation of written contractual provisions must be grounded in the text and read in light of the entire contract (Sattva, at para. 57, relying on G. R. Hall, Canadian Contractual Interpretation Law (2nd ed. 2012), at pp. 15 and 30-32). Surrounding circumstances, including “knowledge that was or reasonably ought to have been within the knowledge of both parties at or before the date of contracting”, may be considered in interpreting the terms of a contract, although they may not overwhelm the contract’s express words

paragraphs.summary: Court states contractual interpretation must be grounded in text and entire contract; surrounding circumstances considered but not overwhelm express words.

propositions.text: Supervising judge concluded IRSSA terms require IAP Documents to be highly confidential, with limited disclosure and eventual destruction.
propositions.quote: The supervising judge concluded that the express terms of the IRSSA provided that the IAP Documents “would be treated as highly confidential but subject to the very limited prospect of disclosure during a retention period and then the documents, including Canada’s copies, would be destroyed”

paragraphs.summary: Supervising judge found IRSSA terms require IAP Documents to be highly confidential with limited disclosure and eventual destruction.

propositions.text: IRSSA preamble aims for fair, comprehensive, lasting resolution and promotes healing, education, truth, reconciliation, commemoration.
propositions.quote: The preamble to the IRSSA states that it aims to provide “a fair, comprehensive and lasting resolution of the legacy of Indian Residential Schools” and to promote “healing, education, truth and reconciliation and commemoration”.

propositions.text: IRSSA main components include IAP provisions in Schedule D and TRC provisions in Schedule N.
propositions.quote: There are several main components to the IRSSA, including provisions bearing on the IAP (in Sch. D) and on the TRC (in Sch. N).

propositions.text: Schedule D requires hearing participants to sign confidentiality agreements.
propositions.quote: Schedule D requires hearing participants to sign confidentiality agreements, confirming that the evidence disclosed is confidential.

propositions.text: Schedule D does not expressly state if federal legislation applies to IAP documents but refers to treatment of information and documents.
propositions.quote: While Sch. D does not expressly state whether federal legislation will apply to documents created or uncovered by the IAP, it does refer to the intended treatment of various types of information and documents

propositions.text: Article III(o) restricts disclosure of hearing information, use of recordings and transcripts, subject to claimant's option to archive transcript.
propositions.quote: Article III(o) restricts disclosure of information from hearings and the use of audio recordings and transcripts, subject to the claimant’s option to deposit the transcript in an archive: o. Privacy i. Hearings are closed to the public. Parties, an alleged perpetrator and other witnesses are required to sign agreements to keep information disclosed at a hearing confidential, except their own evidence, or as required within this process or otherwise by law. Claimants will receive a copy of the decision, redacted to remove identifying information about any alleged perpetrators, and are free to discuss the outcome of their hearing, including the amount of any compensation they are awarded. ii. Adjudicators may require a transcript to facilitate report writing, especially since they are conducting questioning. A transcript will also be needed for a review, if requested. Proceedings will be recorded and will be transcribed for these purposes, as well as if a Claimant requests a copy of their own evidence for memorialization. Claimants will also be given the option of having the transcript deposited in an archive developed for the purpose.

propositions.text: Appendix II item (i) requires claimants to sign confidentiality declaration as part of application.
propositions.quote: Appendix II, item (i) requires claimants to sign a declaration which includes confidentiality provisions as part of their application form

propositions.text: Appendix II item (iv) restricts use of IAP applications; copies other than government-held destroyed unless claimant requests retention.
propositions.quote: Appendix II, item (iv) restricts the use of IAP applications: iv. The following conditions apply to the provision of the application to the Government or a church entity: • The application will only be shared with those who need to see it to assist the Government with its defence, or to assist the church entities with their ability to defend the claim or in connection with their insurance coverage; . . . • Copies will be made only where absolutely necessary, and all copies other than those held by the Government will be destroyed on the conclusion of the matter, unless the Claimant asks that others retain a copy, or unless counsel for a party is required to ret

paragraphs.summary: Supervising judge found IRSSA preamble aims for fair resolution; Schedule D requires confidentiality; provisions restrict disclosure and use of IAP documents.

propositions.text: Schedule N details TRC mandate and principles including victim-centeredness, confidentiality, and no harm.
propositions.quote: Schedule N of the IRSSA details the mandate and process of the TRC. It identifies the TRC’s work as built on principles which include being “victim-centered”, providing “confidentiality (if required by the former student)”, and “do[ing] no harm”.

propositions.text: TRC tasked with creating historical record and promoting awareness and education about residential schools.
propositions.quote: Generally, the TRC is tasked with creating a complete historical record of the residential schools system, and promoting awareness and public education of Canadians about the residential schools system and its impacts

paragraphs.summary: Supervising judge found Schedule N details TRC mandate as victim-centered, confidential, no harm, creating historical record and promoting awareness.

propositions.text: Survivors' stories in the IAP are shared only voluntarily, as emphasized in Sch. N Articles 2(c), 4(b), and 11.
propositions.quote: Another principle — that survivors’ stories will be shared only when done so voluntarily — is frequently emphasized in Sch. N. Article 2 (c) provides that the TRC cannot “compel . . . participation”. Article 4 (b) states that “the truth and reconciliation process is committed to the principle of voluntariness with respect to individuals’ participation”. Article 11 provides that, “[i]nsofar as agreed to by individuals affected and as permitted by process requirements, information from the [IAP] . . . may be transferred to the [TRC] for research and archiving purposes.”

propositions.text: Federal privacy, access to information, and archiving legislation apply to records held by the TRC.
propositions.quote: Federal privacy, access to information, and archiving legislation are expressly stated to apply to records held by the TRC.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that survivors' stories are shared only voluntarily per Sch. N Articles, and federal privacy laws apply to TRC records.

propositions.text: The supervising judge found the IAP was intended to be confidential and private, and that confidentiality was essential for its function.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge found that the negotiators of the IRSSA intended the IAP to be a confidential and private process, that claimants and alleged perpetrators relied on the confidentiality assurances and that, without such assurances, the IAP could not have functioned.

propositions.text: The court finds the supervising judge's findings on confidentiality are free of palpable and overriding error and inescapable given the evidence.
propositions.quote: these findings are not only free of palpable and overriding error, they are simply inescapable in light of the evidence submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found the IAP was confidential and essential for function; the court agrees these findings are inescapable and error-free.

propositions.text: The National Chief emphasized strict confidentiality so only survivors access their own stories.
propositions.quote: The National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations at the time of the IRSSA’s negotiation emphasized that strict confidentiality of the IAP was intended as part of the agreement so that “nobody except the survivor would have access to the story of the survivor”

propositions.text: IAP claimants attested they understood information disclosed would not be shared outside the IAP process.
propositions.quote: IAP claimants who tendered affidavits attesting to their understanding that information disclosed within the IAP would not be shared outside of that process.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found the National Chief and claimants understood IAP confidentiality ensured only survivors access their stories.

propositions.text: Church defendants required confidentiality assurances to participate in the IAP.
propositions.quote: Confidentiality was also crucial to the participation of the church defendants.

propositions.text: The Chancellor of the Archdiocese stated confidentiality assurance was vital inducement to enter the agreement.
propositions.quote: the Chancellor of the Archdiocese of Halifax-Yarmouth stated that the assurance of confidentiality of all the IAP Documents was a vital inducement to his archdiocese entering the agreement.

propositions.text: The former General Superior said her congregation would not have participated if IAP information could become public.
propositions.quote: it would not have done so were there the slightest possibility that information disclosed within the IAP information could become public.

paragraphs.summary: The supervising judge found church defendants required confidentiality assurances to participate in the IAP.

propositions.text: The Chief Adjudicator stated confidentiality is often the key factor in whether a claim proceeds.
propositions.quote: The current Chief Adjudicator stated that confidentiality is a central concern to participants and is often the “key factor” in whether a claim proceeds

propositions.text: Claimants said they would not have participated without assurances of complete confidentiality.
propositions.quote: Claimants have said that they would not have participated in the IAP without assurances of complete confidentiality.

propositions.text: The director of Settlement Agreement Operations West confirmed claimants' concerns were allayed by confidentiality assurances.
propositions.quote: those concerns were allayed by assurances of confidentiality

propositions.text: Confidentiality assurances were important to securing alleged perpetrators' participation in IAP claims.
propositions.quote: Assurances of confidentiality were also important to securing the participation of alleged perpetrators in IAP claims

paragraphs.summary: Affidavits confirm confidentiality assurances were crucial for claimants and alleged perpetrators to participate in the IAP.

propositions.text: IAP information disclosed is highly sensitive, including detailed acts of abuse and resulting harms.
propositions.quote: the amount of compensation depends on the number of “Compensation Points” applicable to proven acts of abuse and the resulting harm that they establish...

propositions.text: Compensable acts range from fondling to repeated anal/vaginal intercourse and serious dysfunction harms.
propositions.quote: At the lower range of the spectrum of abuse are acts such as “One or more incidents of fondling or kissing”... At the top of the table of compensable acts of abuse are “Repeated, persistent incidents of anal or vaginal intercourse”... The highest level of compensable harm is “Continued harm resulting in serious dysfunction”

propositions.text: Additional compensation points apply for aggravating factors like humiliation or degradation.
propositions.quote: Additional compensation points can be allocated to proven harm if certain “Aggravating Factors” are present, such as humiliation or degradation.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the highly sensitive nature of IAP information, detailing acts of abuse and harms compensated.

propositions.text: Claimants' reluctance to disclose sensitive information without confidentiality assurances is understandable.
propositions.quote: the reluctance of claimants to undergo questioning by an adjudicator on these topics without assurances of absolute confidentiality is fully understandable.

propositions.text: An affidavit states such records are unprecedented in sensitivity and scope in Canadian class actions or reparations inquiries.
propositions.quote: Rarely, if ever, in Canadian history has such a broad range of extremely sensitive records been demanded from so many claimants as part of a class action suit or a comparable compensation or reparations inquiry

propositions.text: Inuit Representatives described IAP dossiers as very dark and partial biographies of claimants' lives.
propositions.quote: a dossier created in an IAP claim amounts to “a very dark and very partial biography” of a claimant’s life “from a very young age to the time of the hearing”

propositions.text: Disclosure of IAP information could devastate claimants, witnesses, families, and cause community discord.
propositions.quote: disclosure of information contained in the IAP Documents could be devastating to claimants, witnesses, and families. Further, disclosure could result in deep discord within the communities

propositions.text: Student-on-student abuse claims raise unique privacy and safety risks within First Nations communities.
propositions.quote: student-on-student claims raise unique and heightened privacy and serious safety risks within First Nations communities if the confidential information were to be released

propositions.text: Disclosure of alleged student-on-student abusers' identities would have devastating long-term consequences in communities.
propositions.quote: if there were cases where survivors are alleged to have abused other children... this would have long term devastating consequences in our communities

propositions.text: Assurance that student-on-student abuse names never be made public was a compromise protection in the Settlement Agreement.
propositions.quote: The assurance that this information would never be disclosed outside of the IAP process and the guarantees in the Settlement Agreement were the protections that we obtained as a compromise in the Settlement Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court and affidavits explain the extreme sensitivity of IAP records and the devastating impact of disclosure, especially for student-on-student abuse claims.

propositions.text: The Guide was referred to as extrinsic evidence in interpreting the IRSSA but its utility was contested.
propositions.quote: the Guide was referred to by the supervising judge as extrinsic evidence in his interpretation of the IRSSA. Its utility, however, was contested by the various parties before this Court.

propositions.text: The Guide aids parties in understanding IAP qualification and application but is not part of the IRSSA and contains a disclaimer.
propositions.quote: The Guide is a document intended to aid parties in understanding if they qualify for the IAP, and to help parties fill out the IAP application form. It does not form part of the IRSSA, and indeed it displays at the outset a prominent disclaimer stating that the IAP is governed by Sch. D of the IRSSA and that, in the event of any differences between the Guide and Sch. D, the official document will prevail.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Guide was used as extrinsic evidence but is not part of the IRSSA and its utility was contested.

propositions.text: Appendix B of the Guide explains how federal privacy, access, and archiving laws apply to IAP personal information.
propositions.quote: Appendix B of the Guide, titled “Protection of your personal information”, purports to explain how federal privacy, access, and archiving legislation applies to personal information adduced in an IAP claim.

propositions.text: The Guide defines personal information, security levels, and describes the Privacy Act and Access to Information Act protections and exceptions.
propositions.quote: Definition of personal information... Level of security... Privacy and information laws... Collection of personal information... Use of your personal information... Sharing your personal information with others

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes Appendix B of the Guide explaining federal privacy laws and protections for IAP personal information.

propositions.text: The court would not disturb the supervising judge’s finding that the IRSSA provided for destruction of the IAP Documents.
propositions.quote: we would not disturb the supervising judge’s finding that the IRSSA provided for the destruction of the IAP Documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court would uphold the supervising judge's finding that the IRSSA provides for destruction of the IAP Documents.

propositions.text: IRSSA text on disposition of IAP Documents is unclear; confidentiality is mandated but disclosure allowed as required by law.
propositions.quote: art. III(o) of Sch. D provides that information disclosed at an IAP hearing is confidential, but may be disclosed “as required within this process or otherwise by law”.

propositions.text: Transcripts and recordings have limited use, except claimants may deposit transcripts in an archive.
propositions.quote: Transcripts and recordings may only be used for limited purposes, all of which are specific to the IAP claim, except for the claimant’s option to deposit the transcript in an archive.

propositions.text: Appendix II states copies of applications held outside government must be destroyed after conclusion.
propositions.quote: Appendix II, item (iv) of Sch. D states that all copies of applications “other than those held by the Government will be destroyed on the conclusion of the matter”.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRSSA's unclear text on IAP Documents disposition, confidentiality with limited disclosure, and destruction of non-government copies.

propositions.text: Canada argues federal privacy, access, and archives laws apply to IAP Documents based on IRSSA provisions.
propositions.quote: Canada points to two bases for the application of federal privacy, access, and archives legislation in Sch. D: the reference in art. III(o) to disclosure of information disclosed at IAP hearings as required “otherwise by law”; and the proviso in App. II, item (iv) to the effect that Canada’s copies of applications will not be destroyed at the conclusion of the matter.

propositions.text: The supervising judge found these provisions refer to use in criminal or child welfare proceedings and retention during a retention period.
propositions.quote: The supervising judge...concluding that they refer to the potential use of such information in criminal or child welfare proceedings, and that Canada’s copies of the application forms should be held during a retention period for this purpose.

propositions.text: The court finds no palpable and overriding error in the supervising judge’s interpretation of these provisions.
propositions.quote: In light of the text of the IRSSA and the circumstances surrounding it, the supervising judge’s finding does not evidence a palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: It is unlikely drafters intended these provisions to implicitly link IRSSA to federal privacy, access, and archiving legislation.
propositions.quote: In our view, it is unlikely that the drafters intended these words as a trail of breadcrumbs implicitly linking the IRSSA to federal privacy, access, and archiving legislation

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues federal laws apply to IAP Documents; the supervising judge and court find no error but doubt drafters intended implicit linkage.

propositions.text: IRSSA does not expressly provide disposition for IAP decisions beyond claimants receiving redacted copies.
propositions.quote: the IRSSA does not expressly provide a disposition for IAP decisions, beyond stating that claimants will receive a redacted copy.

propositions.text: Other copies of IAP decisions will not be preserved or archived to maintain confidentiality and disclosure restrictions.
propositions.quote: the necessary implication of this is that other copies of the decisions will not be preserved or eventually archived.

propositions.text: Use and disclosure restrictions on application forms and hearing information apply similarly to IAP decisions.
propositions.quote: The purpose of restricting the use and disclosure of the IAP application forms and the information adduced at hearings would be defeated were IAP decisions... not subjected to similar restrictions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IRSSA does not provide for archiving IAP decisions beyond redacted copies to claimants, preserving confidentiality.

propositions.text: The Guide's significance was contested; it mentions federal laws but guarantees narrower disclosure circumstances.
propositions.quote: While the Guide does mention expressly the application of the federal privacy, access, and archival legislation to the IAP Documents, it also appears to guarantee an exhaustive set of circumstances where personal information is disclosed, which circumstances are markedly narrower than the rights of access under the federal legislation.

propositions.text: The Guide is not part of IRSSA, has a disclaimer, and reproduces privacy provisions from a prior document.
propositions.quote: Given the clear disclaimer at the outset of the Guide... and that its drafters apparently reproduced the privacy provisions from a similar document used in the former ADR process

propositions.text: The court ascribes no interpretive weight to the Guide and finds no error in omitting its references to federal laws in IRSSA interpretation.
propositions.quote: we ascribe no interpretive weight to the Guide. It follows that the supervising judge committed no error by omitting to import the Guide’s references to federal access, privacy, and archiving legislation into the IRSSA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Guide unreliable for interpretation and supports the supervising judge's omission of its federal law references.

propositions.text: Applying the Privacy Act to IAP Documents conflicts with confidentiality and voluntariness principles of the IAP.
propositions.quote: Application of the Privacy Act to the IAP Documents clearly runs counter to the principles of confidentiality and voluntariness upon which... the IAP was founded.

propositions.text: The Privacy Act protects personal information for 20 years after death but allows disclosures during that period.
propositions.quote: The Privacy Act protects personal information from disclosure, but only for 20 years after the death of the relevant individual. Even during the protection period, disclosures of personal information contained in these documents may occur.

propositions.text: The Privacy Act allows individuals access to their personal information, including others' views about them, potentially exposing accusers to alleged perpetrators.
propositions.quote: the Privacy Act provides individuals with a right of access to their personal information, which is defined to include “the views or opinions of another individual about the individual”... this might allow an alleged perpetrator to seek information about their accusers.

propositions.text: Section 8(2)(j) of the Privacy Act permits disclosure of personal information for research or statistical purposes at any time.
propositions.quote: Under s. 8(2)(j) of the Privacy Act , personal information may be disclosed at any time for research or statistical purposes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applying the Privacy Act to IAP Documents conflicts with confidentiality, noting its limited protections and disclosure exceptions.

propositions.text: Retention of IAP Documents in National Archives conflicts with intended absolute confidentiality.
propositions.quote: retention in the National Archives... is inconsistent with the absolute level of confidentiality that the parties intended for these documents.

propositions.text: The supervising judge found federal statutory schemes do not conform to the high confidentiality bargained for by parties.
propositions.quote: the federal access, privacy, and archiving statutory scheme does not conform to the “high degree of confidentiality that the parties bargained for”

propositions.text: Archival and potential disclosure in National Archives conflicts with voluntariness principle of survivor disclosure.
propositions.quote: Nor does archival of the IAP Documents in the National Archives, coupled with their potential disclosure, conform to the principle of voluntariness governing the disclosure by survivors of their stories.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that retaining IAP Documents in National Archives conflicts with confidentiality and voluntariness principles.

propositions.text: Voluntary disclosure principle emerges from IRSSA provisions allowing claimants control over sharing outcomes and participation.
propositions.quote: This principle of voluntary disclosure deserves particular consideration here. It emerges from several of the IRSSA’s provisions... claimants are free to discuss the outcome... may choose to retain a copy... participation... is entirely at the discretion of the claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the IRSSA's principle of voluntary disclosure giving claimants control over their stories and participation.

propositions.text: TRC and NCTR positions to transfer IAP Documents to National Archives would defeat voluntariness principle.
propositions.quote: The position taken by the TRC, and later by the NCTR, that these documents should be transferred to the National Archives and eventually shared with the NCTR, would defeat the principle of voluntariness underlying the IAP.

propositions.text: Disclosure to NCTR and public would conscript survivors' sensitive stories for public education, contrary to parties' bargain.
propositions.quote: their stories... would in time be disclosed to the NCTR... to be applied to its project of commemorating and memorializing the residential schools system... But this is plainly not what the parties bargained for.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority found IRSSA puts survivors in control of their own stories, not Canada or others.
propositions.quote: we agree with the majority at the Court of Appeal that “the IRSSA put the survivors, not Canada and not anyone else, in control of their own stories”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds TRC/NCTR's position to archive IAP Documents would defeat voluntariness and survivors' control over their stories.

propositions.text: NCTR argues destruction of IAP Documents would deny future generations essential knowledge for healing.
propositions.quote: The NCTR’s position is prompted by its stated concern that destruction of the IAP Documents would “deny future generations . . . the collective knowledge and history essential to healing”

propositions.text: NCTR says IRSSA and IAP are flawed because concerns were expressed while wounds are still raw.
propositions.quote: the NCTR says the IRSSA and the IAP are “flawed”

propositions.text: The court says these submissions have no bearing on IRSSA interpretation and it must be interpreted as agreed, not as NCTR wishes.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge was tasked with interpreting the IRSSA as it was agreed to, not as the NCTR would have had the parties agree to.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects NCTR's arguments about future healing and flaws, emphasizing interpretation must follow the agreed IRSSA.

propositions.text: Public commemoration is a core IRSSA objective alongside compensation, but not all components must equally serve both.
propositions.quote: public commemoration of the residential schools system is also a core objective of the IRSSA. That does not mean, however, that each component of the IRSSA must equally contribute to each of those objectives.

propositions.text: The supervising judge found disclosure without consent would compromise IAP's core compensatory function.
propositions.quote: the supervising judge weighed the evidence and found that this core compensatory function would be compromised were the information to be disclosed without claimants’ consent.

propositions.text: The court defers to the fact-finder on the impact of disclosure on compensation function.
propositions.quote: We defer to the fact-finder on that point.

propositions.text: TRC and NCTR have already collected over 7,000 survivor statements, fulfilling commemoration objectives.
propositions.quote: because of the past work of the TRC and the ongoing work of the NCTR, we do not doubt that the objective of commemoration is being met. Residential schools survivors have already given more than 7,000 statements to the TRC detailing their experiences

propositions.text: IAP claimants may still archive their records with the NCTR if they choose.
propositions.quote: under the terms of the supervising judge’s order, IAP claimants will still have the possibility to archive their records with the NCTR if they wish to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IAP's core function is compensation, defers to the judge on disclosure impact, and notes commemoration is met by TRC/NCTR work.

propositions.text: Canada argued destruction of IAP documents would impede its defense against future claims
propositions.quote: Canada also argued that the destruction of the IAP documents would impede its ability to defend itself against future claims

propositions.text: The IRSSA release in favour of Canada means destruction does not impede defense
propositions.quote: In view of the plain language of the release in favour of Canada contained in the IRSSA (art. 4.06(g)), which operates irrespective of whether the class members availed themselves of the IAP and of whether they received compensation, we are not satisfied that this is the case

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argued destruction would impede defense; court finds IRSSA release means it does not impede defense.

propositions.text: IRSSA allows destruction of IAP documents without palpable and overriding error
propositions.quote: Having concluded, without palpable and overriding error, that the IRSSA allowed for the destruction of the IAP Documents

propositions.text: Supervising judge had to craft an appropriate order balancing confidentiality, memorialization, and survivors' choice
propositions.quote: he had to strike a balance between competing concerns: preserving confidentiality and the need to memorialize and commemorate, all the while respecting the choice of survivors to share (or not share) their stories

propositions.text: Supervising judge's order with 15-year retention and notice program is appropriate balance
propositions.quote: The supervising judge’s order, as modified by the majority of the Court of Appeal, charts an appropriate course between the Scylla of potentially unwanted destruction and the Charybdis of potentially injurious preservation

propositions.text: Destruction order allows claimants to preserve documents during 15-year retention via notice program
propositions.quote: The destruction order is subject to a 15-year retention period, during which claimants may choose to have their IAP Documents preserved and archived

propositions.text: Order may conflict with wishes of deceased claimants who had no preservation option
propositions.quote: this order may be inconsistent with the wishes of deceased claimants who were never given the option to preserve their records

propositions.text: Destruction of some records is lesser injustice than disclosure of records expected to remain private
propositions.quote: the destruction of records that some claimants would have preferred to have preserved works a lesser injustice than the disclosure of records that most expected never to be shared

propositions.text: Supervising judge’s order, as varied by Court of Appeal majority, was appropriate exercise of discretion
propositions.quote: The supervising judge’s order, as varied by the majority of the Court of Appeal, was an appropriate exercise of his discretion

paragraphs.summary: Court finds IRSSA allows destruction; supervising judge's order balancing interests and retention period is appropriate discretion.

propositions.text: Notice program should be carried out by Chief Adjudicator, not TRC or NCTR
propositions.quote: The notice program should be carried out by the Chief Adjudicator, as it does not fall within the mandate of either the TRC or the NCTR

propositions.text: Providing TRC or NCTR info for notice program would breach confidentiality
propositions.quote: it would be inconsistent with a confidential process to provide them with the information necessary for the program

propositions.text: Court supports including ADR process documents in destruction order for consistency and fairness
propositions.quote: we support the direction of the Court of Appeal that the orders should include documents developed in the ADR process

propositions.text: IRSSA intent to consolidate litigation into IAP requires consistent treatment of ADR records and IAP documents
propositions.quote: As the intent of the IRSSA was to consolidate existing litigation into the IAP, consistency and fairness require that the records resulting from that litigation should be treated in the same manner as the IAP Documents

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Chief Adjudicator should run notice program; including ADR documents is consistent with IRSSA intent.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed with costs to Independent Counsel
propositions.quote: We would dismiss the appeal, with costs to the Independent Counsel

propositions.text: Chief Adjudicator should conduct notice program promptly with full cooperation
propositions.quote: We also endorse the entreaties of the courts below that the Chief Adjudicator conduct the notice program without delay and with full cooperation from the parties

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal with costs and orders Chief Adjudicator to promptly conduct notice program with cooperation.
